title: Airborne deployment and autonomous recovery
description: Complementary projects study how small UAVs recover stable flight after release.
introduction: A carrier aircraft could bring small UAVs close to a remote mission, preserving their energy for local sensing and search. Before that concept can be useful, each released vehicle must recover from uncertain attitude and motion. The group studies complementary parts of that recovery problem.

problem.heading: A useful mission starts with a controlled recovery.
paragraphs: A small UAV released into the air may have large attitude errors, non-zero velocity and rapid angular motion. Its first task is to establish a controllable state before beginning the local mission.
This is both a controller problem and a sequencing problem. Detecting free fall, choosing when to activate the motors and transitioning into stabilized flight must work together onboard the vehicle.

approach.heading: Separate the recovery questions and their evidence.
paragraphs: Lorenzo Giordano investigated demanding post-release motion and nonlinear or switching control strategies in simulation. Rodrigo Nishikawa’s tailsitter study uses two recovery stages: first orient thrust to arrest the fall, then recover attitude and altitude, comparing PID and nonlinear model predictive control in simulation.

Sofia Simões implemented an ArduPilot recovery architecture that sequences free-fall detection, motor activation, stabilization and position holding. Its real drop sequence is shown separately from those simulation studies.

Yu Tang Liu’s published graph-policy work follows a learning-based direction, combining normal attitude tracking with aggressive recovery. Its dedicated project page presents the separate policy, training and real-flight evidence.

evidence.label: ArduPilot drop sequence
evidence.text: The onboard recording from Sofia Simões’s work shows a real release/recovery sequence. It is not a standalone validation of Nishikawa’s simulated controller or Liu’s learned policy.

evidence.label: High-speed deployment study
evidence.text: Lorenzo Giordano’s work models post-release motion and compares recovery strategies in simulation.

evidence.label: Two-stage tailsitter study
evidence.text: Rodrigo Nishikawa’s published PID/NMPC recovery comparison is evaluated in simulation. It is not presented as a completed carrier-aircraft release experiment.

evidence.label: Carrier deployment concept
evidence.text: Long-range transport by a carrier aircraft motivates the research. The conceptual mission animation is not treated as evidence of an integrated real carrier deployment.
